title: How lovely!
goal: Describe things and people with adjectives, attach them to nouns with the linker *na/-ng*, and exclaim with *ang*.
bekal: recognize that almost all Tagalog adjectives begin with *ma-*
use the linker *na* or *-ng* correctly between two words
praise and complain with the pattern *ang* + adjective

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Sa Luneta Park
dialogs.intro: Late afternoon at Rizal Park in Manila. Budi is out for a stroll with Ana and her little sister, Mia.

lines.speaker: Mia:
lines.id: The park is lovely, isn't it?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: It really is! Big and clean.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Pero ang init ngayon. Uminom tayo ng malamig na tubig.
lines.id: But it's so hot today. Let's drink some cold water.
lines.literal: but how hot now. drink we of cold that water.

lines.speaker: Mia:
lines.text: May tindahan doon. Mura raw ang buko juice.
lines.id: There's a shop over there. They say the buko juice is cheap.
lines.literal: there-is shop over-there. cheap they-say si coconut juice.

lines.speaker: Mia:
lines.text: Sobrang sarap! At malamig na malamig.
lines.literal: excessively tasty! and cold that cold.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Ang bait ng ate mo, Mia. Siya ang bibili.
lines.id: Your sister is so kind, Mia. She's the one who'll buy.
lines.literal: how kind of older-sister your, Mia. she si the-one-who-will-buy.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Hindi na po. Ako na lang. Mabait din ako!
lines.id: No, ma'am, that's all right. Let me do it. I'm kind too!
lines.literal: no now ma'am. I now only. kind also I!

lines.speaker: Mia:
lines.text: Ang galing ng Tagalog mo, kuya!
lines.id: Your Tagalog is so good, kuya!
lines.literal: how good of Tagalog your, big-brother!

notes: **Ma- is the adjective factory.** Take a root meaning a quality or thing, attach *ma-* in front, and you get an adjective: *ganda* (beauty) → *maganda* (beautiful); *init* (heat) → *mainit*; *dumi* (dirt) → *madumi*; *bait* (kindness) → *mabait*. This pattern covers perhaps eight out of ten adjectives you'll meet. Fun fact: Malay and Indonesian use *ber-* or bare roots for similar things, but the *ma-* idea is shared across many Austronesian languages.

**Ang + root = exclamation.** Notice that Mia says *ang ganda*, not *ang maganda*. In the exclamation pattern the *ma-* prefix is dropped and only the root remains: *ang init!*, *ang sarap!*, *ang bait!*. This is the most common form of praise you'll hear in the Philippines.

**Ng after an exclamation points to its owner.** *Ang ganda ng parke* — "how lovely the park is". The word *ng* here is the second marker of Tagalog, fully set up in unit 5. For now, memorize the whole pattern: *ang* + adjective + *ng* + thing.
**Ano? at the end of a sentence** means "right?" or "isn't it?" — asking for agreement, like English tag questions ("isn't it?"). Another form with the same meaning: *di ba?*
**Oo nga** = "yes, that's true". *Nga* confirms and affirms; it also softens requests (*pakiulit nga* — please repeat, would you).
**Sobrang** (from Spanish *sobra*, excess) is the most common way to say "very": *sobrang init*, *sobrang sarap*, *sobrang bait*. It goes in front of the root, not in front of the *ma-* form.
**Malamig na malamig** — repeating the adjective with the linker *na* in the middle means "very, really". The pattern is like English "cold, cold" or "really really cold".
**Raw / daw** means "they say". *Mura raw* = they say it's cheap. The form is *raw* after a vowel, *daw* after a consonant — the same rule as *rin/din*.
**Hindi na po** literally means "not anymore" and is used to decline an offer gently. Declining with just *hindi* sounds harsh; *na* makes it soft, and *po* makes it polite.

grammars.title: Ma- adjectives and their roots
body: Seeing the root behind an adjective isn't just extra knowledge: it's immediately useful, because the exclamation form and the "very" form use the root, not the *ma-* form.
after: Note *marami* versus *madami*: the standard form is *marami*, because *d* between two vowels becomes *r*. *Madami* is heard in everyday speech and won't cause confusion, but in writing use *marami*.

Not all adjectives start with *ma-*. The most common ones without it: *mura* (cheap), *mahal* (expensive), *bago* (new), *luma* (old, for objects), *matanda* (old, for people), *bata* (young), *masama* (bad), *mabuti* (good).
⚠️ *Mahal* means expensive **and** beloved. *Mahal kita* isn't "you're expensive" but "I love you" — one of the biggest traps for beginners.

grammars.title: The linker na / -ng — Tagalog's glue
body: Whenever two words describe each other in Tagalog, a linker is required between them. The linker has no meaning; its job is only to join. Its form is decided by **the last letter of the first word**.

head: First word ends in
Form
Example
Meaning
rows: a vowel (a, e, i, o, u)

after: The order of adjective and noun is **free to reverse**, as long as the linker adjusts with it: *magandang bahay* and *bahay na maganda* are both correct and equally common.

This linker will appear in every unit that follows — with numbers (*dalawang bata*), with *gusto* (*gusto kong matulog*), and in relative clauses (*ang taong mabait*). If there's one small thing worth drilling until it's automatic, this is it.
The most typical beginner mistake isn't the wrong form, but **forgetting it altogether**: *maganda bahay* sounds to a Filipino like "nicehouse" with no space — understood, but clearly foreign.

blocks.text: *Mahirap* does two jobs at once: "difficult" for things, "poor" for people. Context separates them and it never confuses native speakers: *Mahirap ang Tagalog* (Tagalog is hard) can't possibly be understood as "Tagalog is poor".
Tell the last row apart from the others: *masyado* means **too**, and almost always carries a complaining tone. *Ang sarap* praises food; *masyadong maalat* complains about it.

blocks.title: The opposite: hindi masyado
items: *Hindi masyadong mainit* = "not too hot". The pattern *hindi masyadong* + adjective is the gentlest way to express dislike without offending anyone.
This matters in the Philippines, where open criticism is considered rude. Asked whether the food is good, answering *hindi masarap* sounds harsh; *hindi masyado* is much safer.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right linker: na or -ng.
Turn into an exclamation with ang. Example: Mainit ang araw. → Ang init ng araw!
Put the words in the right order.
items: tubig / malamig / na / uminom / tayo / ng

answers: Magandang bahay. — Malamig na tubig. — Malinis na kwarto. — Ang init! — Ang ganda ng parke. — Masyadong maingay.
Ang ganda ng parke! — Ang sarap ng pagkain! — Ang bait ng guro! — Ang laki ng bahay! — Ang dami ng tao!
Uminom tayo ng malamig na tubig. — Ang ganda ng parke. — Masarap ba iyon? — Mahirap pero masaya. — Masyadong mainit ngayon.
